title: Vector-Valued Functions and Space Curves
lead: A vector-valued function $\kvecr(t)$ assigns a vector to each value of the parameter $t,$ its component functions real-valued functions of $t.$ Graphed in standard position, its vectors trace a plane curve or a space curve such as a helix. This section evaluates such functions, finds their domains, graphs them, and takes their limits component by component.
objectives: Write the general equation of a vector-valued function in component form and unit-vector form.
Recognize parametric equations for a space curve.
Describe the shape of a helix and write its equation.
Define the limit of a vector-valued function.
summary_html:
• A vector-valued function is a function of the form $\kvecr(t)=\kf(t)\;\kveci+\kg(t)\;\kvecj$ or $\kvecr(t)=\kf(t)\;\kveci+\kg(t)\;\kvecj+\kh(t)\;\kveck,$ where the component functions f, g, and h are real-valued functions of the parameter t.
  • The graph of a vector-valued function of the form $\kvecr(t)=\kf(t)\;\kveci+\kg(t)\;\kvecj$ is called a plane curve. The graph of a vector-valued function of the form $\kvecr(t)=\kf(t)\;\kveci+\kg(t)\;\kvecj+\kh(t)\;\kveck$ is called a space curve.
  • It is possible to represent an arbitrary plane curve by a vector-valued function.
  • To calculate the limit of a vector-valued function, calculate the limits of the component functions separately.

exercises.prompt: For the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=(t^{2}-3t)\;\textbf{i}+(4t+1)\;\textbf{j},$ evaluate $\textbf{r}(0),\;\textbf{r}(1),\text{and}\;\textbf{r}(-4).$ Does this function have any domain restrictions?

answer.solution: $\textbf{r}(0)=\textbf{j},\;\textbf{r}(1)=-2\;\textbf{i}+5\;\textbf{j},\;\textbf{r}(-4)=28\;\textbf{i}-15\;\textbf{j}$ The domain of $\textbf{r}(t)=(t^{2}-3t)\;\textbf{i}+(4t+1)\;\textbf{j}$ is all real numbers.
answer.hint: Substitute the appropriate values of t into the function.

exercises.prompt: Create a graph of the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=(t^{2}-1)\;\textbf{i}+(2t-3)\;\textbf{j},$ $0\le t\le 3.$

answer.hint: Start by making a table of values, then graph the vectors for each value of t.

exercises.prompt: Calculate $\lim_{t\to -2}\;\textbf{r}(t)$ for the function $\textbf{r}(t)=\sqrt{t^{2}-3t-1}\;\textbf{i}+(4t+3)\;\textbf{j}+\sin \frac{(t+1)\pi}{2}\;\textbf{k}.$

answer.solution: $\lim_{t\to -2}\;\textbf{r}(t)=3\;\textbf{i}-5\;\textbf{j}-\textbf{k}$
answer.hint: Use Equation 13.4 from the preceding theorem.

exercises.prompt: Give the component functions $x=f(t)$ and $y=g(t)$ for the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=3\;\sec t\;\textbf{i}+2\;\tan t\;\textbf{j}.$

answer.solution: $f(t)=3\;\sec t,g(t)=2\;\tan t$

exercises.prompt: Sketch the curve of the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=3\;\sec t\;\textbf{i}+2\;\tan t\;\textbf{j}$ and give the orientation of the curve. Sketch asymptotes as a guide to the graph.

Given the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle \cos t,\sin t\rangle ,$ find the following values:

a. $\lim_{t\to \frac{\pi}{3}}\;\textbf{r}(t)$

b. $\textbf{r}(\frac{\pi}{3})$

c. Is $\textbf{r}(t)$ continuous at $t=\frac{\pi}{3}?$

d. Graph $\textbf{r}(t).$

answer.solution: a. $\langle \frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\rangle ,$ b. $\langle \frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\rangle ,$ c. Yes, the limit as t approaches $\pi /3$ is equal to $\textbf{r}(\pi /3),$ d.

exercises.prompt:
Let $\textbf{r}(t)=e^{t}\;\textbf{i}+\sin t\;\textbf{j}+\ln t\;\textbf{k}.$ Find the following values:

a. $\textbf{r}(\frac{\pi}{4})$

b. $\lim_{t\to \pi /4}\;\textbf{r}(t)$

c. Is $\textbf{r}(t)$ continuous at $t=\frac{\pi}{4}?$

answer.solution: a. $\langle e^{\pi /4},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\ln (\frac{\pi}{4})\rangle ;$ b. $\langle e^{\pi /4},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\ln (\frac{\pi}{4})\rangle ;$ c. Yes

exercises.prompt:
Find the limit of the following vector-valued functions at the indicated value of t.

$\lim_{t\to \pi /2}\;\textbf{r}(t)$ for $\textbf{r}(t)=e^{t}\;\textbf{i}+\sin t\;\textbf{j}+\ln t\;\textbf{k}$

answer.solution: $\langle e^{\pi /2},1,\ln (\frac{\pi}{2})\rangle$

exercises.prompt:
Find the limit of the following vector-valued functions at the indicated value of t.

$\lim_{t\to e^{2}}\langle t\;\ln (t),\frac{\ln t}{t^{2}},\sqrt{\ln (t^{2})}\rangle$

answer.solution: $2e^{2}\;\textbf{i}+\frac{2}{e^{4}}\;\textbf{j}+2\;\textbf{k}$

exercises.prompt:
Find the limit of the following vector-valued functions at the indicated value of t.

$\lim_{t\to \infty}\;\textbf{r}(t)$ for $\textbf{r}(t)=2e^{-t}\;\textbf{i}+e^{-t}\;\textbf{j}+\ln (t-1)\;\textbf{k}$

answer.solution: The limit does not exist because the limit of $\ln (t-1)$ as t approaches infinity does not exist.

exercises.prompt:
Find the domain of the vector-valued functions.

Domain: $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle t^{2},\tan t,\ln t\rangle$

answer.solution: $t\gt 0,t\ne (2k+1)\frac{\pi}{2},$ where k is an integer

exercises.prompt:
Find the domain of the vector-valued functions.

Domain: $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle \csc (t),\frac{1}{\sqrt{t-3}},\ln (t-2)\rangle$

answer.solution: $t\gt 3,t\ne n\pi ,$ where n is an integer

exercises.prompt:
Let $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle \cos t,t,\sin t\rangle$ and use it to answer the following questions.

Sketch the graph of $\textbf{r}(t).$
For what values of t is $\textbf{r}(t)=2e^{-t}\;\textbf{i}+e^{-t}\;\textbf{j}+\ln (t-1)\;\textbf{k}$ continuous?

answer.solution: All t such that $t\in (1,\infty )$

exercises.prompt:
Eliminate the parameter t, write the equation in Cartesian coordinates, then sketch the graphs of the vector-valued functions.

$\textbf{r}(t)=t^{3}\;\textbf{i}+2t\;\textbf{j}$

answer.solution: $y=2\sqrt[3]{x},$ a variation of the cube-root function

exercises.prompt:
Eliminate the parameter t, write the equation in Cartesian coordinates, then sketch the graphs of the vector-valued functions.

$\textbf{r}(t)=3(\cos t)\;\textbf{i}+3(\sin t)\;\textbf{j}$

answer.solution: $x^{2}+y^{2}=9,$ a circle centered at $(0,0)$ with radius 3, and a counterclockwise orientation

exercises.prompt:
Use a graphing utility to sketch each of the following vector-valued functions:

[T] $\text{r}(t)=(2\;{\cos }^{2}\;t)\;\text{i}+(2-\sqrt{t})\;\text{j}$

Use a graphing utility to sketch each of the following vector-valued functions:

[T] $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle 2-\sin (2t),3+2\;\cos t\rangle$

Find a vector-valued function that traces out the given curve in the indicated direction.

$\textbf{r}(t)=\langle t,t^{2}\rangle ;$ from left to right

answer.solution: For left to right, $y=x^{2},$ where t increases

exercises.prompt:
Consider the curve described by the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=(50e^{-t}\cos t)\;\textbf{i}+(50e^{-t}\sin t)\;\textbf{j}+(5-5e^{-t})\;\textbf{k}.$

What is the initial point of the path corresponding to $\textbf{r}(0)?$

Consider the curve described by the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=(50e^{-t}\cos t)\;\textbf{i}+(50e^{-t}\sin t)\;\textbf{j}+(5-5e^{-t})\;\textbf{k}.$

[T] Use technology to sketch the curve.

Consider the curve described by the vector-valued function $\textbf{r}(t)=(50e^{-t}\cos t)\;\textbf{i}+(50e^{-t}\sin t)\;\textbf{j}+(5-5e^{-t})\;\textbf{k}.$

Eliminate the parameter t to show that $z=5-\frac{r}{10}$ where $r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}.$

answer.solution: With $x=50e^{-t}\cos t$ and $y=50e^{-t}\sin t,$ $x^{2}+y^{2}=2500e^{-2t}(\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t)=2500e^{-2t},$ so $r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}=50e^{-t}$ and $e^{-t}=\frac{r}{50}.$ Substituting into the third component, $z=5-5e^{-t}=5-5\cdot\frac{r}{50}=5-\frac{r}{10}.$ The curve lies on the cone $z=5-\frac{r}{10},$ which it climbs from $(50,0,0)$ toward its apex $(0,0,5)$ as $t\to\infty.$

exercises.prompt: [T] Let $r(t)=\cos t\;\textbf{i}+\sin t\;\textbf{j}+0.3\;\sin (2t)\;\textbf{k}.$ Use technology to graph the curve (called the roller-coaster curve) over the interval $[0,2\pi ).$ Choose at least two views to determine the peaks and valleys.
Use the results of the preceding two problems to construct an equation of a path of a roller coaster with more than two turning points (peaks and valleys).

answer.solution: One possibility is $r(t)=\cos t\;\textbf{i}+\sin t\;\textbf{j}+\sin (4t)\;\textbf{k}.$ By increasing the coefficient of t in the third component, the number of turning points will increase.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

A parametric equation that passes through points P and Q can be given by $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle t^{2},3t+1,t-2\rangle ,$ where $P(1,4,-1)$ and $Q(16,11,2).$

answer.solution: False. At $t=1,$ $\mathbf{r}(1)=\langle 1,4,-1\rangle,$ which is $P.$ For $\mathbf{r}(t)$ to be $Q(16,11,2)$ we would need $t^{2}=16,$ $3t+1=11$ and $t-2=2$ at once, that is $t=\pm 4,$ $t=\frac{10}{3}$ and $t=4,$ and no single $t$ satisfies all three. At $t=4$ the curve is at $\langle 16,13,2\rangle,$ not $Q.$ The curve passes through $P$ but not through $Q.$

exercises.prompt:
Find the domains of the vector-valued functions.

$\textbf{r}(t)=\langle e^{t},\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-t}},\sec (t)\rangle$

answer.solution: $t\lt 4,$ $t\ne \frac{n\pi}{2}$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-r207"></sup>

exercises.prompt:
Sketch the curves for the following vector equations. Use a calculator if needed.

[T] $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle \sin (20t)e^{-t},\cos (20t)e^{-t},e^{-t}\rangle$

Find a vector function that describes the following curves.

Intersection of the cone $z=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ and plane $z=y-4$

answer.solution: $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle t,2-\frac{t^{2}}{8},-2-\frac{t^{2}}{8}\rangle$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-r211"></sup>

footnotes.html: The book prints $\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\;\mathbf{i}+\sin t\;\mathbf{j},$ “a unit circle centered at the origin”. Eliminating the $\mathbf{k}$ component of $\mathbf{r}(t)=4\cos t\;\mathbf{i}+4\sin t\;\mathbf{j}+t\;\mathbf{k}$ leaves $4\cos t\;\mathbf{i}+4\sin t\;\mathbf{j},$ the circle of radius 4 centered at the origin.

The key prints $t\ne \frac{n\pi}{2}.$ Of the three components only $\sec t$ is undefined anywhere other than $t\ge 4,$ and only at the odd multiples of $\frac{\pi}{2}$: the domain is $t\lt 4,$ $t\ne \frac{(2n+1)\pi}{2},$ where $n$ is an integer.

This curve satisfies $z^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$ and $z=y-4,$ but its $z=-2-\frac{t^{2}}{8}$ is negative: it is where the plane meets the lower nappe $z=-\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}.$ On the cone $z=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ as printed, $z\ge |y|\gt y-4,$ so the cone and the plane do not meet.
